What Lecture 9 gave us, stated as one object — the feedback law:

u=γ(t,x),and in the one closed form,u=−Kx,K=R−1B⊤Pu = \gamma(t,x), \qquad\text{and in the one closed form,}\qquad u = -Kx, \quad K = R^{-1}B^\top Pu=γ(t,x),and in the one closed form,u=−Kx,K=R−1B⊤P

And three ways to obtain it — HJB, Riccati, Pontryagin. All three are exact. All three take fff (or A,BA,BA,B) as an input, and we no longer have it.

What we keep, and what we lose

The feedback law survives. The dynamics do not.

Everything else follows from removing fff. Three things break the moment it vanishes:

  • The solvers. HJB is a PDE in fff; the Riccati equation is built from AAA and BBB; Pontryagin needs ∂xf\partial_x f∂x​f to run the costate backwards. None of the three can even be written down.
  • The pointwise minimisation. Every one of them ends in min⁡u∈U{ g+∂xV⋅f }\min_{u\in U}\{\,g + \partial_x V\cdot f\,\}minu∈U​{g+∂x​V⋅f} — a search over a continuum that needs fff to evaluate. Lecture 8 met the same object as max⁡a′Q(s′,a′)\max_{a'}Q(s',a')maxa′​Q(s′,a′) and could not do it either.
  • The rollout. We cannot integrate x˙=f\dot x = fx˙=f to see what a candidate controller would do. We can only run it and watch.
So stop trying to compute the best action. If you cannot search for the best action, learn to output it.

One honest detour — why not identify the system?

The most literal idea, and the exact rhyme of the detour Lecture 8 took: estimate the dynamics from data, then run Lecture 9 unchanged.

(A^,B^)=arg min⁡A,B ∑t∥xt+1−Axt−But∥2⟹solve the Riccati equation for K^(\hat A,\hat B) = \argmin_{A,B}\ \sum_t \big\lVert x_{t+1} - Ax_t - Bu_t \big\rVert^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{solve the Riccati equation for } \hat K(A^,B^)=A,Bargmin​ t∑​​xt+1​−Axt​−But​​2⟹solve the Riccati equation for K^

This is system identification, it is the oldest idea in adaptive control, and it is perfectly valid.

But notice the same waste Lecture 8 noticed. To act we only ever need the controller — m×nm\times nm×n numbers, or one network — yet here we first estimate a whole dynamics model, and then we act as though it were true. Why estimate fff at all,

when we could estimate the controller directly?

That question — skip the model, learn the thing that acts — is the entire policy-based programme, and it is Lecture 8's question with Q∗Q^*Q∗ replaced by πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​. (The model comes back, deliberately and learned, in Lecture 11.)

The roadmap — four questions

One question per Act. This strip returns at every transition — watch the highlight move.

Q1 Gradient?Q2 Variance?Q3 Continuous?Q4 Safe step?
  • Q1 — How do we get a gradient without fff? The score-function trick: the dynamics enter the trajectory's law and leave its log-derivative. (Williams, 1992; Sutton et al., 2000)
  • Q2 — Why is the estimate so noisy? Causality, baselines, the advantage — and the actor–critic. (Mnih et al., 2016)
  • Q3 — How do we handle continuous control? DPG / DDPG: the actor climbs ∇aQ\nabla_a Q∇a​Q instead of searching it. (Silver et al., 2014; Lillicrap et al., 2015)
  • Q4 — How large a step dare we take? Trust regions in policy space: TRPO and PPO. (Schulman et al., 2015; 2017)

The score-function trick — the dynamics vanish

One identity does all the work:   ∇p=p ∇log⁡p\;\nabla p = p\,\nabla \log p∇p=p∇logp. It turns the gradient of an expectation into an expectation of a gradient:

∇θEτ∼pθ[R(τ)]=∫∇θpθ(τ)R(τ) dτ=∫pθ(τ) ∇θlog⁡pθ(τ) R(τ) dτ=Eτ∼pθ[∇θlog⁡pθ(τ) R(τ)]\nabla_\theta \E_{\tau\sim p_\theta}[R(\tau)] = \int \nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau)R(\tau)\,d\tau = \int p_\theta(\tau)\,\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)\,R(\tau)\,d\tau = \E_{\tau\sim p_\theta}\big[\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)\,R(\tau)\big]∇θ​Eτ∼pθ​​[R(τ)]=∫∇θ​pθ​(τ)R(τ)dτ=∫pθ​(τ)∇θ​logpθ​(τ)R(τ)dτ=Eτ∼pθ​​[∇θ​logpθ​(τ)R(τ)]

Now expand that log. The product becomes a sum, and every term without θ\thetaθ differentiates to zero:

∇θlog⁡pθ(τ)=∇θlog⁡μ(s0)⏟= 0+∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)+∑t∇θlog⁡P(st+1∣st,at)⏟= 0  =  ∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau) = \underbrace{\nabla_\theta\log\mu(s_0)}_{=\,0} + \sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t) + \underbrace{\sum_t\nabla_\theta\log \hl{P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)}}_{=\,0} \;=\; \sum_{t}\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)∇θ​logpθ​(τ)==0∇θ​logμ(s0​)​​+t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)+=0t∑​∇θ​logP(st+1​∣st​,at​)​​=t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)
The start distribution and the dynamics contribute exactly zero to the gradient.

This is the precise sense in which fff is "deleted": we never needed it. Where Lecture 9 solved the dynamics, here they simply drop out of the algebra — the policy's own log-probability is all that is left. We still live in the dynamics; we just never differentiate through them.

Reading the estimator — it is weighted maximum likelihood

Put the two halves together and the whole of Act 1 is one line:

∇θJ(θ)=Eτ∼πθ[(∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st))⏟∇θJML(θ)  −  make this trajectory likelier (∑trt)⏟how good it was]\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \E_{\tau\sim\pi_\theta}\Big[\underbrace{\Big(\textstyle\sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\Big)}_{\hl{\nabla_\theta J_{\mathrm{ML}}(\theta)} \;-\; \text{make this trajectory likelier}}\ \underbrace{\Big(\textstyle\sum_t r_t\Big)}_{\text{how good it was}}\Big]∇θ​J(θ)=Eτ∼πθ​​[∇θ​JML​(θ)−make this trajectory likelier(∑t​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​))​​ how good it was(∑t​rt​)​​]

The first factor, alone, is the gradient of the log-likelihood of the trajectory — the maximum-likelihood gradient of Lecture 2, the direction that would make this trajectory more probable. The return simply weights it.

  • Increase the likelihood of trajectories with large accumulated reward;
  • decrease the likelihood of trajectories with small accumulated reward.
Policy gradient is imitation of your own better moments, reweighted by how well they went.

There is no arg max⁡\argmaxargmax anywhere in that sentence, and no model. It is also, exactly, Lecture 6's move — a generative model trained to emit the good samples — one axis over.

The policy gradient theorem, and REINFORCE

The dynamic-programming route (Backup 1) reaches the same place through QπQ^\piQπ rather than through trajectories, and gives the canonical statement:

∇θJ(θ)=Eπθ[ ∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)  Qπθ(s,a) ]\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \E_{\pi_\theta}\big[\,\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a\mid s)\; Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)\,\big]∇θ​J(θ)=Eπθ​​[∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)Qπθ​(s,a)]

REINFORCE makes it runnable by replacing the unknown QπQ^\piQπ with the return actually observed, since Eπ[Gt∣s,a]=Qπ(s,a)\E_\pi[G_t\mid s,a] = Q^\pi(s,a)Eπ​[Gt​∣s,a]=Qπ(s,a): (Williams, 1992)

θ←θ+α∑tγt ∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)  Gt\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \sum_{t} \gamma^t\,\nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\; G_tθ←θ+αt∑​γt∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)Gt​

Written per action, per episode, or averaged over a batch of NNN episodes — the source deck writes all three. The γt\gamma^tγt is usually dropped in practice, and we drop it from here on.

It is unbiased — the estimator's mean is the gradient. And it is Monte Carlo, so we must wait for the episode to end, and every one of the TTT terms is multiplied by the same noisy tail. Unbiased and badly high variance. Taming that is Act 2.

ACT 2Taming variance with a criticLecture 10

Why the estimate is so noisy

Q1 Gradient?Q2 Variance?Q3 Continuous?Q4 Safe step?

Look again at what one episode contributes:

g^(i)=(∑t=0T−1∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st))(∑t=0T−1rt)\hat g^{(i)} = \Big(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\Big)\Big(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} r_t\Big)g^​(i)=(t=0∑T−1​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​))(t=0∑T−1​rt​)

Every score term is multiplied by the same scalar — the whole episode's return. One unlucky tail rescales all TTT of them together. And the return itself is a sum of TTT random rewards along a random trajectory.

Worse, it is credit assignment by superstition: an action at t=1t=1t=1 is rewarded for something that happened at t=40t=40t=40 and could not possibly have caused.

Three corrections follow, and every one of them leaves the mean untouched.

That constraint is the whole game. Anything that changes the mean changes what we are optimising; only variance is free to attack. ("no bias, high variance — reduce the variance while keeping the bias unchanged", the source deck's own framing)

Fix 1 — causality: half the terms were pure noise

An action at time ttt cannot affect a reward at time t′<tt' < tt′<t. So those cross-terms have mean zero and contribute nothing but variance. Drop them:

∇θJ=E[∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st) ∑t′≥trt′]  =  E[∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)  Q^t]\nabla_\theta J = \E\Big[\sum_{t}\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\ \hl{\sum_{t'\ge t} r_{t'}}\Big] \;=\; \E\Big[\sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\;\hat Q_t\Big]∇θ​J=E[t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​) t′≥t∑​rt′​]=E[t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)Q^​t​]

The inner sum is the reward-to-go Q^t\hat Q_tQ^​t​ — an unbiased sample of Qπ(st,at)Q^\pi(s_t,a_t)Qπ(st​,at​), which is why the trajectory derivation and the DP derivation meet here.

The cost of this fix is one index. It is the cheapest variance reduction in reinforcement learning, and in the numbers of the Act 1 widget it removes about half.

ACT 2Taming variance with a criticLecture 10

Two dials on the same ideawhat the field does with the actor–critic once it has one

  • A3C / A2C — run many actors in parallel on separate copies of the environment. At any instant they occupy different states, so their data is decorrelated without a replay buffer: parallelism plays the role of replay, and lets the method stay on-policy. (Mnih et al., 2016)
  • nnn-step returns — bootstrap after nnn steps rather than at the end:   Rt=∑i=1nγi−1rt+i−1+γnV(st+n)\;R_t = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma^{i-1}r_{t+i-1} + \gamma^{n}V(s_{t+n})Rt​=∑i=1n​γi−1rt+i−1​+γnV(st+n​). REINFORCE is n=Tn=Tn=T, one-step actor–critic is n=1n=1n=1.
  • GAE — do not pick nnn; average all of them geometrically,   A^tGAE(γ,λ)=∑l≥0(γλ)l δt+lV\;\hat A_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)} = \sum_{l\ge0}(\gamma\lambda)^l\,\delta^V_{t+l}A^tGAE(γ,λ)​=∑l≥0​(γλ)lδt+lV​. (Schulman et al., 2016)
GAE is TD(λ\lambdaλ) for the advantage — Lecture 8's bias–variance dial, moved from the value to the thing that trains the policy.

Act 3

Continuous control: DDPG

Q3. Lecture 8 handed over a wall. This is where it falls.
ACT 3Continuous control: DDPGLecture 10

The wall Lecture 8 left

Q1 Gradient?Q2 Variance?Q3 Continuous?Q4 Safe step?

The source deck states the debt in one sentence: "although DQN solves problems with high-dimensional observation spaces, it can only handle discrete and low-dimensional action spaces". There are exactly two ways to put a continuous action into a Q-network, and both break.

Option 1 — discretise the action

One output head per action, as in DQN. Take −1≤a≤1-1\le a\le 1−1≤a≤1 and cut it into bins of width Δa\Delta aΔa.

What is a good Δa\Delta aΔa? Coarse bins mean poor control resolution; fine bins mean ndn^dnd heads for ddd joints. And the optimum is never exactly on the grid.

Option 2 — feed the action in

One network Qw(s,a)Q_w(s,a)Qw​(s,a) with the action as an input, so the action stays continuous.

But the update needs max⁡a′Qw(s′,a′)\max_{a'}Q_w(s',a')maxa′​Qw​(s′,a′), and QwQ_wQw​ is non-convex in a′a'a′. That is a global optimisation, at every transition, forever.

Option 1 keeps the update and breaks the action space; option 2 keeps the action space and breaks the update. There is no third way that keeps Q-learning, which is why the answer has to come from the other lineage.

The wall, measured

One state, one continuous action, and the critic's Q(s,⋅)Q(s,\cdot)Q(s,⋅) across it. Nine bins already cost 96=531,4419^6 = 531{,}44196=531,441 evaluations per transition on a six-joint arm — and still miss the peak by 0.160.160.16. Twenty-one bins close the gap and cost 85,766,121. The actor emits its action in one forward pass and refines it by following ∇aQ\nabla_a Q∇a​Q: cheap, and only ever local — move its start and watch it settle on the wrong hill, which is honest, and is why TD3 and SAC exist.

The deterministic fix — the actor climbs the critic

Make the actor deterministic, a=μθ(s)a = \mu_\theta(s)a=μθ​(s), and let it ascend the critic's action-gradient: (Silver et al., 2014)

∇θJ(μθ)=Es∼ρμ[ ∇θμθ(s)  ∇aQ(s,a)∣a=μθ(s)]\nabla_\theta J(\mu_\theta) = \E_{s\sim\rho^\mu}\Big[\,\nabla_\theta \mu_\theta(s)\;\nabla_a Q(s,a)\big|_{a=\mu_\theta(s)}\Big]∇θ​J(μθ​)=Es∼ρμ​[∇θ​μθ​(s)∇a​Q(s,a)​a=μθ​(s)​]
This is how the intractable max⁡aQ\max_a Qmaxa​Q is finally beaten: the actor follows ∇aQ\nabla_a Q∇a​Q uphill instead of searching for its summit.

Determinism is not a stylistic preference. Compare the Bellman expectation in the two cases:

Qπ(st,at)=Er,s′∼E[r+γ Ea′∼π[Qπ(s′,a′)]]versusQμ(st,at)=Er,s′∼E[r+γ Qμ(s′,μ(s′))]Q^\pi(s_t,a_t) = \E_{r,s'\sim E}\big[r + \gamma\,\hl{\E_{a'\sim\pi}}[Q^\pi(s',a')]\big] \qquad\text{versus}\qquad Q^\mu(s_t,a_t) = \E_{r,s'\sim E}\big[r + \gamma\,Q^\mu(s',\mu(s'))\big]Qπ(st​,at​)=Er,s′∼E​[r+γEa′∼π​[Qπ(s′,a′)]]versusQμ(st​,at​)=Er,s′∼E​[r+γQμ(s′,μ(s′))]

With a deterministic μ\muμ the inner expectation disappears and only the environment is left inside the expectation. Two consequences, both decisive: the critic can be trained off-policy on any data at all, and there is one integral to estimate instead of two — less variance.

ACT 3Continuous control: DDPGLecture 10

A deterministic actor explores nothing

A deterministic policy has no randomness to explore with, and the obvious repair — act uniformly at random — is a poor one. The source deck gives three reasons, and the third is unusual in this course:

  • random actions drive the policy update into regions where the critic is not accurate (Lecture 5's adversarial-optimiser hazard, in an RL costume);
  • exploring unseen states needs action that is consistent along the episode, not resampled each step;
  • and on real hardware, random jittering breaks the machine.
The pendulum argumentthe source deck's own picture

Swinging a pole upright takes a sustained push in one direction, then alternation near the top. White noise averages to nothing over an episode and never sustains anything, so a uniformly random policy might eventually find the swing-up — after enormously many samples.

Hence the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process,  dxt=−κ xt dt+σ dWt\,dx_t = -\kappa\,x_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_tdxt​=−κxt​dt+σdWt​, added to μθ(s)\mu_\theta(s)μθ​(s): noise that is temporally correlated, so exploration pushes rather than jitters.

Act 4

Stepping without falling

Q4. We have a gradient and we have tamed its variance. How far along it dare we step?
ACT 4Stepping without fallingLecture 10

The step-size trap unique to RL

Q1 Gradient?Q2 Variance?Q3 Continuous?Q4 Safe step?

In supervised learning a bad step costs one bad update; the next minibatch arrives from the same fixed dataset and pulls you back. In RL it is worse, because

the policy generates its own next batch of data.

A step that pushes πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ too far lands in a region where the policy is bad — and now every subsequent sample comes from that bad policy. The gradient estimated there points somewhere else again. The damage is self-reinforcing, and there is no fixed dataset to fall back on.

This is also why the parameter step size is the wrong thing to control. A tiny change in θ\thetaθ can produce a large change in behaviour (a softmax near saturation), and a large one can produce none at all. What must be bounded is the distance between the old and new action distributions.

Maximise an importance-weighted advantage, subject to staying inside a KL ball around the policy that collected the data: (Schulman et al., 2015)

max⁡θ E[πθ(a∣s)πθold(a∣s) A^]s.t.E[DKL(πθold(⋅∣s) ∥ πθ(⋅∣s))]≤δ⇒monotonic improvement\max_{\theta}\ \E\Big[\frac{\pi_\theta(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a\mid s)}\,\hat A\Big] \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \E\big[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid s)\,\|\,\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s)\big)\big] \le \delta \qquad\Rightarrow\quad \hl{\text{monotonic improvement}}θmax​ E[πθold​​(a∣s)πθ​(a∣s)​A^]s.t.E[DKL​(πθold​​(⋅∣s)∥πθ​(⋅∣s))]≤δ⇒monotonic improvement

The ratio is Act 2's off-policy importance weight, reused: the data is from πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}πθold​​, the objective is about πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​. Solved by linearising the objective and quadratising the KL through the Fisher matrix — a natural-gradient step (Backup 5). Powerful, and heavy.

PPO — the clip that does the same job for nothing

TRPO's constraint is exact and expensive. PPO keeps the intent and throws away the machinery: with r(θ)=πθ(a∣s)/πθold(a∣s)r(\theta) = \pi_\theta(a\mid s)/\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a\mid s)r(θ)=πθ​(a∣s)/πθold​​(a∣s), (Schulman et al., 2017)

JCLIP(θ)=E[min⁡( r(θ) A^,  clip(r(θ), 1−ϵ, 1+ϵ) A^ )]J^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta) = \E\Big[\min\big(\,r(\theta)\,\hat A,\ \ \mathrm{clip}\big(r(\theta),\,1-\epsilon,\,1+\epsilon\big)\,\hat A\,\big)\Big]JCLIP(θ)=E[min(r(θ)A^,  clip(r(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^)]

No second-order machinery, no conjugate gradient, no line search. When the ratio leaves [1−ϵ,1+ϵ][1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon][1−ϵ,1+ϵ] in the direction the update was pushing it, the objective goes flat and the incentive to push further is simply removed.

With shared actor–critic parameters the practical objective adds two terms — −c1(Vθ(s)−Vtarget)2-c_1(V_\theta(s)-V_{\text{target}})^2−c1​(Vθ​(s)−Vtarget​)2 for the critic and +c2H(πθ(⋅∣s))+c_2 H(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s))+c2​H(πθ​(⋅∣s)), an entropy bonus for exploration. The entropy term is the seed of maximum-entropy RL and of SAC.

The clip, and the asymmetry nobody mentions

The clipped objective as a function of the ratio, for a good action (A^>0\hat A>0A^>0) and a bad one (A^<0\hat A<0A^<0). Read the slopes: for A^>0\hat A>0A^>0 the gradient is exactly zero above 1+ϵ1+\epsilon1+ϵ — no reward for making a good action still likelier. For A^<0\hat A<0A^<0 it is zero below 1−ϵ1-\epsilon1−ϵ but stays alive above 1+ϵ1+\epsilon1+ϵ: an action already too probable and known to be bad keeps being pushed down. The clip only removes the incentive that would take you out of the region.

What we hand on

Lecture 10 leavesthe trust-region machinery — a KL ball, and a clip
Lecture 11 puts the model backlearned, and lets the two lineages rejoin

The trust region travels further than it looks. It is Lecture 1's ratio test in behaviour space; it is what makes PPO the default workhorse of modern policy-based RL; and it is the discipline every method needs the moment its own output decides what it will see next — which is exactly the condition Lecture 12 will face with no interaction at all.

Lecture 11 asks the question both extensions have been avoiding: if deleting the model cost us this much, what happens if we learn it — and plan with it, and let an optimal-control teacher train a policy student?

Lecture 9 found the feedback law by solving the dynamics. Lecture 10 finds the same law by sampling its gradient.
The dynamics never solved, only experienced — and the controller learned, not derived.
Questions?
Read against Lecture 8's closing and the symmetry is exact: value-based RL kept the Bellman equation and threw away the model; policy-based RL kept the feedback law and threw away the dynamics. Two parents, one orphaning move. And the through-line of every algorithm today is a single expression, E[∇θlog⁡πθ⋅A^]\E[\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta\cdot\hat A]E[∇θ​logπθ​⋅A^] — they differ only in which advantage they trust and how large a step they dare.

with g=∇θLg=\nabla_\theta Lg=∇θ​L and HHH the Fisher information matrix. The KL has zero gradient at θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}}θold​, which is why its leading term is quadratic.

Step 2 — a linear objective on an ellipsoid. The maximiser lies along the natural-gradient direction H−1gH^{-1}gH−1g, scaled to the KL radius:

θnew=θold+2δ g⊤H−1g   H−1g\theta_{\mathrm{new}} = \theta_{\mathrm{old}} + \sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{\,g^\top H^{-1}g\,}}\;H^{-1}gθnew​=θold​+g⊤H−1g2δ​​H−1g

Step 3 — practice. H−1gH^{-1}gH−1g is obtained by conjugate gradient without ever forming HHH, and the step is backtracked until the true KL and the true improvement both hold — which is Lecture 1's accept-or-shrink test, verbatim.

PPO discards all of it and recovers the effect with one clip on r(θ)r(\theta)r(θ). That is the usual pattern in this course: an exact method that characterises the answer, and a cheap one that reaches it — HJB and LQR, TRPO and PPO.
